nodes.label: ScientistTwo: Pioneering the Human Knowledge Frontier with Autonomous AI
nodes.description: An autonomous research pipeline combines experiments, ablations and simulated peer review; its reported successes require careful attention to selection and evaluation.

nodes.label: Self-Organizing Agent Teams Learn to Reason Together
nodes.description: Frozen teams learn reusable coordination strategies, with gains depending partly on their ability to recognize correct reasoning.

nodes.label: Solipsistic Superintelligence is Unlikely to be Cooperative
nodes.description: Argues that cooperative AI must account for adaptive counterparts, institutions and human agency rather than optimize in isolation.

nodes.label: Some Simple Economics of AGI
nodes.description: Develops an economic argument that verification capacity and responsibility become scarce as automated execution becomes cheaper.

nodes.label: Artificial intelligence in drug discovery—what it is, where we stand and the path forward
nodes.description: Calls for evaluating AI by its contribution to better drug-development decisions and patient-relevant outcomes.

nodes.label: Reflecting on 25 years of cancer research: transformative advances and unmet expectations
nodes.description: Six researchers reflect on cancer biology, translational disappointments and opportunities for human–AI co-science.

nodes.label: The scientific paper needs an uncertainty layer
nodes.description: Proposes attaching reusable qualifications and uncertainty records to scientific claims as humans and AI reuse them.

nodes.label: Why LLMs Aren’t Scientists Yet: Lessons from Four Autonomous Research Attempts
nodes.description: Four autonomous ML research attempts expose implementation drift, weak evaluation and failures of scientific judgment.

nodes.label: A Case Study on Emergent Cheating and Whistleblowing in Autonomous Research Swarms
nodes.description: A mathematical research swarm illustrates how shared infrastructure can spread both verifier exploits and organized resistance.

nodes.label: Eliciting Research Taste in LLMs through Future Research Direction Choice
nodes.description: Studies model preferences among future research directions using order-controlled pairs, without equating agreement with scientific merit.

nodes.label: Drug Discovery Has No Magic Wands
nodes.description: Daphne Koller argues that useful AI drug discovery depends on better measurements and causal understanding of human biology.

nodes.label: Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini in the Real-World
nodes.description: Reports multi-agent research workflows across materials, biology and computing, with different levels of autonomy and validation.

nodes.label: Anthropic uses Claude to formalize proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem
nodes.description: Reports on AI-assisted formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem and the role of shared proof infrastructure.

nodes.label: Medical school lab scientists get a new partner: AI
nodes.description: Describes medical researchers integrating specialized AI agents with vetted data, laboratory workflows and human oversight.

nodes.label: Latent-space reasoning as a third axis of test-time scaling
nodes.description: François Chollet highlights latent iterations alongside longer reasoning and parallel exploration.

nodes.label: The paradox at the heart of AI and science
nodes.description: Terence Tao discusses scientific understanding, human learning and the limits of accelerating answer production.

nodes.label: Imagining a new future for science
nodes.description: Eunice Jun explores representations and interfaces that make scientific reasoning more inspectable.

nodes.label: AI Infrastructure at Periodic
nodes.description: Describes infrastructure for long scientific tool runs, specialized models and efficient training; performance claims come from the company.

nodes.label: AI in Science: Early Insights
nodes.description: Combines model-use data, a specialist-model inventory and a researcher survey to examine adoption, time savings and verification demands.

nodes.label: A beginning for mathematics
nodes.description: Distinguishes producing mathematical results from cultivating human understanding, and proposes rewarding research programs, learning and community-building as AI capabilities grow. A constructive essay on preserving scientific values and complementary human–AI inquiry.

nodes.label: Mathematics is effectively dead
nodes.description: A critical response to Litt focused on provenance, credit, accountable authorship and open mathematical discourse; its claims about private-data reuse and opaque proof workflows are conditional or speculative.

nodes.label: Why I didn’t sign the Fields medallists’ letter
nodes.description: Timothy Gowers defends a plurality of mathematical motivations, including problem-solving, while arguing that preserving the institutions supporting shared understanding matters more than restricting the supply of AI-generated results.

nodes.label: Why I agreed to join AGMAI
nodes.description: Martin Hairer explains his decision to join the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, describes its independence and advisory limits, and argues for engagement with AI labs to improve scholarship and represent community concerns.

nodes.label: The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery
nodes.description: Wraps off-the-shelf coding agents in an explicit research loop, with pre-registered rubrics, parallel workers sharing a memory and ablations of the winning program, so they behave less like hyperparameter optimizers. Sakana reports an ALIFE 2026 oral on Error Diffusion with humans setting questions and verifying claims, plus autonomous gains on Doc-to-LoRA retrieval and learned evolution strategies.

nodes.label: The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated AI Research, Now Published in Nature
nodes.description: Sakana, UBC, Vector and Oxford report in Nature on the AI Scientist, whose v2 wrote a paper that passed blind review at an ICLR 2025 workshop before being withdrawn. Its ensembled automated reviewer matches human reviewer accuracy on OpenReview decisions. The authors list naive ideas, weak rigour, hallucinated citations and a compute-only scope as limits, and call for watermarking and community norms.

nodes.label: AGMAI
nodes.description: Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence.

nodes.label: Fields medallists’ letter
nodes.description: An open letter from Fields medallists on AI and mathematics, discussed by Gowers.

nodes.label: Verification as the bottleneck
nodes.description: As producing results gets cheaper, checking them and owning responsibility for them becomes the scarce resource.

nodes.label: Understanding vs. answers
nodes.description: The value of science lies partly in humans understanding results, not only in results existing.

nodes.label: Research taste
nodes.description: Judgment about which questions and directions are worth pursuing.

nodes.label: Credit and provenance
nodes.description: Who did the work, where ideas and data came from, and who is accountable.

nodes.label: Scientific institutions
nodes.description: Journals, prizes, departments and communities that sustain shared understanding.

nodes.label: Uncertainty records
nodes.description: Machine-reusable qualifications attached to scientific claims.

nodes.label: Autonomous research agents
nodes.description: Pipelines where AI systems plan, run and write up research with little human input.

nodes.label: Multi-agent coordination
nodes.description: How teams or swarms of agents divide labour, communicate and check each other.

nodes.label: Verifier exploits and reward hacking
nodes.description: Agents gaming the checker instead of solving the problem; can spread through shared infrastructure.

nodes.label: Test-time scaling
nodes.description: Spending more compute at inference: longer reasoning, parallel exploration, latent iteration.

nodes.label: Formalization of proofs
nodes.description: Turning human proofs into machine-checked proofs.

nodes.label: Measurement and causal biology
nodes.description: Better data about human biology as the real constraint on AI drug discovery.

nodes.label: Inspectable scientific reasoning
nodes.description: Representations and interfaces that let people see and challenge how a conclusion was reached.

nodes.label: Implementation drift
nodes.description: Agents silently changing the experiment they were asked to run.

nodes.label: Decision-relevant evaluation
nodes.description: Judging AI by whether it improves real decisions and outcomes, not benchmark scores.

nodes.label: Selection effects in reported wins
nodes.description: Showcased successes may be cherry-picked from many attempts.

nodes.label: Learned coordination strategies
nodes.description: Frozen models learning reusable ways to coordinate as a team.

nodes.label: The Agentic Scientist
nodes.description: Sakana's scaffold that orchestrates coding agents through hypothesis, rubric-based evaluation, shared memory and ablation stages.

nodes.label: The AI Scientist (v1, v2)
nodes.description: Sakana's earlier end-to-end automated research systems, the predecessors of the Agentic Scientist.

nodes.label: Coding agents (Codex, Claude Code)
nodes.description: Agents that carry out long software tasks on their own.

nodes.label: AutoIllustrate
nodes.description: A pipeline for scientific figures that keeps an editable draw.io file as the source of truth, so every diagram can be corrected by hand.

nodes.label: Co-discovery
nodes.description: Humans set the question and the standards of evidence, and agents widen the experiments researchers can run.

nodes.label: Optimizer, not scientist
nodes.description: Coding agents given a research problem tend to push scores up with narrow ideas, without examining why the gains happen.

nodes.label: Error Diffusion
nodes.description: A biologically motivated alternative to backpropagation.

nodes.label: Pre-registered rubrics
nodes.description: Evaluation criteria fixed before any experiment runs.

nodes.label: Parallel workers with shared memory
nodes.description: Workers test hypotheses in parallel and pool successes and failures.

nodes.label: ICLR 2025 ICBINB workshop
nodes.description: The “I Can’t Believe It’s Not Better” workshop, where an AI Scientist-v2 paper averaged 6.33 in blind review.

nodes.label: Automated Reviewer
nodes.description: An ensemble of five LLM reviews following NeurIPS guidelines, reported at 69% balanced accuracy on OpenReview decisions.

nodes.label: Norms for AI-generated papers
nodes.description: Watermarking, disclosure, withdrawal and IRB review for research written by AI.
